platform.why: Why it is built this way

infrastructure.name: Infrastructure
infrastructure.title: One server, production rules
infrastructure.intro: The whole platform lives on one VPS running K3s. Cloudflare sits in front, everything else is closed.
how: Cloudflare proxy in front, port 443 open only to Cloudflare ranges, with Authenticated Origin Pulls
SSH and the Kubernetes API reachable only over Tailscale
nftables firewall, SSH hardening and unattended upgrades from bootstrap scripts
Cloudflare DNS, TLS, redirects, R2 buckets and the GitHub org itself described in Terraform
trade: One node: a hardware failure takes everything down. Recovery is drilled instead of paying for a second node
Kernel updates wait for a manual reboot at a quiet hour
proof: etcd snapshots and Postgres backups go to Cloudflare R2
A written recovery runbook with RPO and RTO targets
infrastructure.reason: I wanted to own every layer, so the whole platform runs on one small server: cheap to keep, nothing hidden behind a managed service, and every failure is mine to understand. Recovery is drilled instead of paying for a second node.

gitops.name: GitOps & CI
gitops.title: Deploy is a merged pull request
gitops.intro: Nothing is applied to the cluster by hand. The cluster follows a public Git repository.
how: A service merges to master, CI builds an image and pushes it to GHCR by digest
A bot opens a PR in gitops with the new digest, I read the diff and merge
Argo CD syncs the cluster, then a smoke check runs against production
Every service calls the same reusable org workflows by tag, no copy-pasted pipelines
trade: A human merge on every deploy is slower, and that is on purpose
The gitops repo is public, so only Sealed Secrets live there
proof: Nightly failure tests: 28 scenarios against the deployed set
Branch rulesets on master: PR and approval, no bypass
gitops.reason: Every change to the cluster is a reviewed pull request. Rolling back is a git revert, and the history shows who changed what and why.

starters.name: Starters
starters.why: A new service in an afternoon
starters.title: New services start from a template
starters.intro: Two starters and two full examples. A new service starts small and copies only the capabilities it needs.
how: next-starter: SEO, EN and RU, strict CSP with nonce, shadcn/ui, health probes, Vitest, Playwright and axe
nest-starter: config, JSON logs, health, metrics, Postgres with Drizzle, Zod validation, OpenAPI
next-example and nest-example hold the rest: API proxy, TanStack Query, Redis, pg-boss jobs, RabbitMQ with outbox
One service contract: port, user, probes, limits and time budgets every image must follow
trade: Shared code is copied, not imported, until several services really need it as a package
proof: Starters and examples are verified in CI on every change
Integration tests run against real Postgres with Testcontainers
starters.reason: Every service starts from the same template, so on day one it already has health checks, logs, metrics, tests and a deploy pipeline instead of getting them in week three.

identity.name: Identity
identity.why: One sign-in, no tokens in the browser
identity.title: One sign-in for every site
identity.intro: id.nick-lukashik.com signs people in once; the other sites sign in through it and keep their own session.
how: Sign-in by email code, Google or passkey
Short ES256 access tokens, five minutes, checked by every API against JWKS
Refresh tokens rotate; reusing an old one ends the session
The browser never sees a token: the session is a sealed HttpOnly cookie
trade: A lost response during refresh is handled explicitly instead of logging the person out
Rate limits on email codes, so a mail quota cannot lock everyone out
proof: End-to-end tests for sign-in across two sites and refresh races
identity.reason: Sign-in is the part people trust you with the most, so it gets the strictest rules: short-lived tokens, rotation, and nothing sensitive reachable from JavaScript.

events.name: Events
events.why: Nothing lost between DB and broker
events.title: Events that never get lost
events.intro: Services talk through RabbitMQ, and no event is lost between the database and the broker.
how: The event is written to an outbox table in the same transaction as the data
A relay publishes the outbox to RabbitMQ
Consumers record every message in an inbox, so a repeat is applied once
Failed messages go to a dead-letter queue and can be replayed with one command
trade: At-least-once delivery, so every handler has to be idempotent
More tables and moving parts than a plain HTTP call
proof: Nightly tests stop RabbitMQ, Postgres and Redis and check that nothing is lost
events.reason: Distributed systems break in the gaps between services. The outbox and inbox close those gaps, and nightly tests prove it by breaking things on purpose.

payments.name: Payments & wallet
payments.title: Money that adds up
payments.intro: A coin wallet with an append-only ledger, and a payment service in front of it.
how: Append-only ledger with double entry; rows are never updated or deleted
Every credit and debit carries a reference, so a retry cannot pay twice
Webhooks check the provider signature first and the amount against the order snapshot
Reconciliation against the wallet and against the provider
trade: The payment service is built but not live yet: the provider is still being chosen
proof: Tests for duplicate references, truncation attempts and replayed webhooks
payments.reason: Money code has to be boring: append-only, idempotent, reconciled. A retry, a replayed webhook or a crash halfway through can never create or lose a coin.

llm-gateway.name: LLM gateway
llm-gateway.title: Every model behind one API
llm-gateway.intro: A shared service that gives every project the same OpenAI-compatible API to several models.
how: /v1/chat/completions and /v1/models, JSON schema output, reasoning effort per call
Synchronous calls and background jobs for long ones
A key per client with an allow-list of models, plus a network policy
Full request log kept for 14 days, then deleted
trade: Runs as a single replica because of the provider sign-ins, an exception to the platform rule
proof: Other services on the platform call it in production
Request log kept for 14 days, then deleted automatically
llm-gateway.reason: Every project wants an LLM, and none of them should deal with keys, limits and providers on its own. One gateway gives them the same API and one place to log and control usage.

observability.name: Observability
observability.title: I know before users do
observability.intro: Metrics, logs and alerts live in the cluster and talk to me in Telegram.
how: kube-prometheus-stack for metrics and alert rules, each alert with a runbook
Loki and Alloy for logs, stored in R2
Alerts go to a Telegram topic; a dead man's switch pings Healthchecks every few minutes
Argo CD reports a degraded app to the same chat
trade: Some alerts are still noisy, and tuning them is ongoing work
proof: Alert rules have unit tests in CI
observability.reason: If something breaks, I want to know before anyone else does. Every alert has a runbook, and the monitoring lives in the same cluster as the services it watches.

meta.title: Blog
meta.description: Notes from production: what broke on my platform, how I fixed it, and the things I build along the way.

blog.title: Notes from production
blog.intro: What broke on my platform, how I fixed it, and the things I build along the way. Written for engineers, short enough to read with a coffee.

alerts-noise.title: My alerts channel screamed every four hours
alerts-noise.lead: Two alerts kept firing in Telegram all weekend. Neither meant the site was down, and that is exactly the problem.
tldr: NodeRebootRequired: the server installs security updates itself but never reboots itself, so the alert repeats every 4 hours until someone does.
AlertmanagerFailedToSendAlerts: one lost “I am alive” ping out of four to Healthchecks is 25%, and the default rule calls that critical.
An alert that fires and then resolves itself ten minutes later teaches you to ignore alerts. That is worse than no alert.

body.p: Over two days the ops topic got NodeRebootRequired roughly every four hours, plus a CRITICAL AlertmanagerClusterFailedToSendAlerts that resolved itself ten minutes later, several times. On the same night the nightly failure tests went red once.

Unattended upgrades install security patches on the node. Some of them, usually the kernel, only take effect after a reboot. The node is configured to never reboot by itself: a single-node cluster that restarts at a random moment is an outage I did not schedule.

So a small timer writes node_reboot_required to the node-exporter textfile collector, and an alert fires after 24 hours. Alertmanager then repeats it every repeat_interval, which is four hours. The fix is boring: reboot at a quiet hour, check the nodes and the site.

Alertmanager has two receivers. Telegram worked the whole time. The other one is a dead man's switch: every four minutes the cluster pings Healthchecks, and if the pings stop, Healthchecks tells me the whole monitoring stack is gone.

One ping in a window of four timed out on the way out. 1 of 4 is 25%, 1 of 3 is 33%, 1 of 2 is 50%: exactly the numbers in the messages. The rule from kube-prometheus-stack treats any failure towards a critical integration as critical.

ul: Reboots go into a fixed weekly window instead of waiting for me to notice.
The send-failure rule for the dead man's switch only fires when pings fail for a sustained period, not on a single timeout.
Argo CD gets a recovered message too, so a Degraded alert is never left hanging.

body.p: The rule I keep coming back to: every alert must mean “do something now”. If the honest answer is “wait, it will pass”, it is not an alert, it is a log line.

liquid-logo.title: Turning one AI image into a live 3D logo
liquid-logo.lead: The NL on the first screen started as a single picture from ChatGPT. Here is how it learned to write itself.
tldr: A real 3D model of the letters looked like an inflated balloon. The picture already had the material I wanted, so I animated the picture.
From the image I compute the stroke centre lines, the order a pen would write them in, and a relief. Three small textures drive one shader.
The result keeps the exact look of the render, still turns in 3D and draws itself in about two seconds.

body.p: I traced the calligraphy into curves and swept a tube along them. Technically correct, visually wrong: smooth tubes, rings where strokes met, and none of the liquid chrome that made the original image good.

body.h: Keep the picture, add the data

body.p: So I went the other way. Codex generated the same monogram on a transparent background. From its alpha I build a distance field, find the centre line of each of the three pen strokes and assign every pixel to a stroke and a position along it.

ul: Texture one: surface normals and a relief height, from the distance field.
Texture two: which stroke a pixel belongs to and how far along it is.
Texture three: a smooth depth per stroke, so loops pass in front of each other when the logo turns.

body.p: A shader compares each pixel's position along its stroke with the pen's progress. Behind the pen the metal swells up from nothing, wobbles and settles. A bead of liquid rolls at the tip and throws small drops that bounce on the floor.

A light drifts above the logo, so the highlights move by themselves. The floor is a dark water mirror: sharp right under the letters, broken by slow ripples further out. The cursor tilts the piece and sends a ripple through the metal.

failure-tests.title: Breaking my platform on purpose, every night
failure-tests.lead: Each night a robot stops Postgres, RabbitMQ, Redis and mail under my real services and checks that nothing is lost.
tldr: The images under test are the exact digests deployed to production, started together in Docker Compose.
Scenarios: database down, broker down, Redis down, SMTP down, concurrent sign-ins, replayed payment webhooks, and a log check.
The result lands in Telegram before I wake up.

body.p: Unit tests prove a function works. They do not prove that a sign-in survives the broker restarting in the middle of it. That kind of bug only shows up when real services fail in real order.

A scheduled GitHub Actions workflow in the gitops repository reads the image digests from the production manifests, starts the whole set with Postgres, Redis, RabbitMQ and a fake mail server, and runs Playwright scenarios against it.

ul: postgres-down: requests fail fast and the service recovers when the database is back.
broker-down: events wait in the outbox and are delivered later, once.
smtp-down: sign-in codes are retried, never logged.
payment-replay: the same webhook twice credits the wallet once.

body.p: Serial, no retries, strict timeouts: a slow runner can turn it red. That is a trade I accept. A flaky red run costs me five minutes; a hidden race in production costs much more.

privacy.title: Privacy
privacy.intro: nick-lukashik.com and its account services (the account at id.nick-lukashik.com, the coin wallet and payments) are run by Nick Lukashik, an independent engineer. This page says what data they handle, why, and how you stay in control.

sections.title: What is collected and why
items: Account: your email address, an optional display name and your language, to sign you in and to write to you about your account.

Sign-in: one-time email codes, stored only as a keyed hash and valid for ten minutes. The email address a code was requested for is kept with it, readable, also when no account exists yet. With Google sign-in: your Google account ID, email address and name. With a passkey: its public key, its ID, a name such as “Chrome on macOS”, technical details of the authenticator (its model ID, transports, backup state and use counter), and when it was added and last used. Your fingerprint or face never leaves your device.

Sessions: for each one, the browser and operating system, the IP address, how you signed in, and the time of sign-in and of last activity, to protect the account and to show you where you are signed in.

Wallet and payments: your coin balance and its history, and for each payment the pack, the amount, the currency, the status and the payment provider’s reference. Card details are entered on the provider’s page and never reach this platform.
Notifications: the messages in your account inbox and the emails sent to you (sign-in codes, a welcome message, receipts).
These sites: statistics of visits through Google Analytics (see “Who else processes data”) and no advertising. Server logs with IP addresses are kept for 30 days for security and troubleshooting.

sections.title: Cookies
items: nl_locale: your language, for the whole nick-lukashik.com domain, kept for one year.
__Secure-nl_session, for the whole nick-lukashik.com domain: your session, encrypted. It is HttpOnly, so scripts cannot read it, and lives for thirty days.
__Host-id_login and __Host-id_google at id.nick-lukashik.com: a sign-in in progress. They live for ten minutes and are deleted when sign-in is complete.

__Host-id_passkey at id.nick-lukashik.com: the ID and the name of the passkey last used in this browser (such as “Chrome on macOS”), encrypted, so the sign-in page can offer it straight away. Kept for one year, also after you sign out. It goes when you remove that passkey in this browser, or when a sign-in finds that the passkey no longer exists.
Cloudflare, which delivers the sites, may set its own security cookies such as __cf_bm to tell people from bots.
_ga and _ga_*: cookies of Google Analytics, two years. Set from the first visit.
nl_consent: a mark that you pressed “OK” on the statistics banner, for the whole nick-lukashik.com domain, kept for one year. It only hides the banner.
All of them but the statistics cookies are needed for the sites to work.

sections.title: Who else processes data
items: The hosting provider of the server the platform runs on.
Cloudflare: every request passes through its network, which protects and delivers the sites. It also runs the domain name system and stores encrypted backups.
Google: only if you choose to sign in with Google. It shares your account ID, email address, whether the email is verified, and your name.
An email delivery service, for sign-in codes, welcome messages and receipts.

Google Analytics, through Google Tag Manager: statistics of visits to the sites from the first visit. Google receives the time of the visit, the pages, where you came from, your device, your approximate location and your IP address.

Telegram: a daily summary of those statistics goes to the site owner’s private group. It has the number of visitors and pages viewed, the pages and where visitors came from, and for visits from a marked link also the time, source, campaign, city, country, device and length of the visit. It has no names, email addresses or IP addresses.
A payment provider: takes payments, once there are any.

sections.title: How long it is kept
items: Account data stays until you ask to delete the account.

Inbox messages stay until the account is deleted. Your coin balance and its history count as payment records and stay after that too. Records of emails sent hold no address and no text, only a request or payment reference, the template and the status, and are deleted 90 days after the last attempt to send.

Sign-in codes expire after ten minutes and are deleted after 24 hours. A session ends thirty days after its last activity at the latest; ended sessions are kept for 90 days to investigate misuse, then deleted.
Payment records are kept as long as accounting rules require.
Server logs: 30 days. Backups are encrypted and replaced on a rolling basis.

sections.title: Your choices
items: Change your name and language, add or remove passkeys, link or unlink Google and end sessions in your account at id.nick-lukashik.com.
The sites always collect statistics and have no switch for it. You can limit them in your browser, by blocking cookies or Google's scripts.
To get a copy of your data or to delete your account, write to the contact below.

sections.title: Changes
items: If this policy changes in a meaningful way, this page and the date at the top are updated before the change takes effect.

terms.title: Terms of service
terms.intro: These terms apply to nick-lukashik.com and its account services (id.nick-lukashik.com, the coin wallet and payments), run by Nick Lukashik. Creating an account means you accept them.

sections.title: The account
items: You sign in with a code sent to your email, a passkey or Google. Whoever controls your email or your devices can sign in, so keep them safe.
You can end any of your sessions in the account, and delete the account on request.

sections.title: Coins
items: Coins are a virtual unit for the platform’s apps. They have no cash value: they cannot be withdrawn, exchanged for money or sent to another person.
Payments are not open yet. Once they are, the packs are 100 coins for $1, 550 for $5 and 1200 for $10, or the price shown in rubles or euros. You pay the price you saw at checkout.

Coins are credited once the payment provider confirms the payment. A purchase is final once the coins are credited, unless the law of your country gives you a right to a refund. If something went wrong with a payment, write to the contact below.

sections.title: Subscriptions
items: Once subscriptions are available, a subscription gives extra features for the period paid. When the period ends without a renewal, the features end too.

sections.title: Fair use
items: Do not try to break the services or other people’s use of them, get into accounts that are not yours, or abuse sign-in or payments with automated tools. An account that does may be suspended.

sections.title: The service as it is
items: The services are run by one engineer and provided as they are. Every effort goes into keeping them running and your data safe, but they may sometimes be unavailable or contain errors.
Nothing in these terms takes away rights that the law gives you and that cannot be waived.

sections.title: Changes
items: If these terms change in a meaningful way, this page and the date at the top are updated before the change takes effect.
